title: Pesto Genovese Pasta
author: Marco Bellini
desc: Pesto Genovese Pasta brings together Liguria's fragrant basil sauce — pounded with pine nuts, garlic, Parmigiano, and Pecorino — with pasta, green beans, and potatoes in one classic pot.
longDesc: True Genovese pesto is traditionally made with a mortar and pestle, which bruises rather than purees the basil, preserving its bright flavor without the bitterness a food processor's blade can introduce through heat and oxidation.
ingredients: 150 g (5 oz) green beans, trimmed and halved
60 g (2 cups packed) fresh basil leaves
120 ml (½ cup) extra virgin olive oil
equipment: Mortar and pestle or food processor
steps: Make the pesto: in a mortar and pestle (or food processor), pound or pulse the basil, pine nuts, and garlic with a pinch of salt until a coarse paste forms.
Gradually work in the Parmigiano and Pecorino, then slowly drizzle in the olive oil, mixing until you have a thick, vibrant green sauce. Set aside.
Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Add the diced potatoes and cook for 5 minutes.
Add the green beans and pasta to the same pot, cooking together until the pasta is al dente.
Reserve a cup of pasta water, then drain the pasta, potatoes, and beans together.
Toss everything with the pesto in a large bowl, off the heat (never over direct heat, which dulls the basil's flavor and color), adding pasta water as needed to loosen.
chefTips: Never cook pesto directly — always toss it with hot pasta off the heat to preserve its bright color and fresh flavor.
A traditional mortar and pestle genuinely produces a better texture and flavor than a food processor, which can heat and oxidize the basil.
The potatoes and green beans are a distinctly Ligurian touch — don't skip them for an authentic version of this dish.
commonMistakes: Heating the pesto directly, which turns it dull and can make it taste bitter.
Over-processing in a food processor, generating heat that darkens the basil.
Omitting the potatoes and green beans, which are a traditional and integral part of this specific dish.
storage: Fresh pesto keeps refrigerated with a layer of olive oil on top for up to 5 days, or freeze for up to 3 months.
reheating: Best served at room temperature or gently warmed pasta tossed with cold pesto — avoid direct heating.
healthBenefits: Basil and olive oil provide antioxidants and healthy fats.
Pine nuts contribute healthy fats and protein.
culturalNote: Genovese pesto has Protected Geographical Indication status, with strict traditional requirements including small-leafed Genovese basil (DOP) and a stone mortar for the most authentic preparation.
